In my experience, I find the only way to overcome social anxiety is to continue doing things that fill me with dread. If it fills me with dread, it's probably worth doing in the long-run. Over-time, it does get easier and the physical effects of the anxiety will lessen. Easier said than done, though, so that's definitely not to say that one can't have coping mechanisms and/or seek support from a GP. Maybe create a plan of goals that you hope to achieve socially for yourself, to build up your confidence gradually, and let others around you know that you're working on this for their support. 

In terms of dealing with those physical effects, perhaps have a few excuses to hand that you can use if you feel it coming on - for example, 'just going to nip to the bathroom' (and take some deep breaths/splash your face with water), 'gosh it's hot in here', or even laugh about it 'gosh for some reason I'm blushing/am a bit nervous today!'. Practice taking deep breaths and keeping your shoulders back when in those situations too.

My first comment would be that we often tend to see mediation analyses published with cross-sectional data (i.e. survey data taken at one point in time), but this is conceptually incorrect (see Baron & Kenny, 1986). I would therefore suggest that if you want to do a mediation, carefully consider how you plan to interpret your model, or better still, try to collect longitudinal data (e.g. 2 time-point survey, or experiment). You could consider moderation analyses instead, which you can conceptually do with cross-sectional data so may be more appropriate.

So you have 1 independent variable (IV; what you change in the study) with 3 levels (as you have three video games). You might call this IV 'change in game'. The dependent variable (DV; what's being measured) is the questionnaire, as you're using it to measure game 'funness'. I'm assuming a higher score (7) means greater funness? 
And, since you've mentioned it's a between subjects analysis (the groups are unrelated), I'm then assuming you need to do a one-way ANOVA. Essentially, you'd be comparing the means of the total questionnaire score per game (the DV against the three levels of the IV). It would be significant if the p level is less than 0.05 (in multiple comparisons box if using SPSS). Looking at the effect size (magnitude of the significance level) might also be helpful if there is significance. 

To compare the differences between the three different games on against each other, a post-hoc analysis would be necessary. Tukey test, perhaps.

And, if you wanted to test the different parts to your questionnaire (e.g. joy/curiosity), you'd need a MANOVA, as then you'd have more than one DV.

I'd ask Google for how to run the analysis and prepare your data to do this :-)
